name: Dabu mud-resist block printing
summary: Dabu is a Rajasthani hand-block technique in which a paste of mud, lime and natural gum is block-printed onto cloth, dusted with sawdust and sun-dried so that it resists a cold indigo bath; resist-and-dye cycles are repeated to build layered shades. Akola village in Chittorgarh district, home to Chhipa printers on the Beduch river, is widely described as its centre of origin. Recipes vary between centres, and in present-day Akola tar-based resists have partly displaced mud.

sources.title: Dabu printing Akola | Story of Indian crafts and craftsmen
sources.author: Gaatha (unattributed)
sources.notes: Craft-organisation field documentation of Akola: legend, Chhipa community, Beduch river settlement, mud+gum+lime paste, indigo, alizarin->naphthol, tar substitution, motifs (Kahma, Lal titri, Dholika, Kantedar), Phetiya garments, Kishangarh fabric, Udaipur pigments.

sources.title: Block Print~Akola (Craft Archive)
sources.author: Gaatha (unattributed)
sources.notes: Detailed cluster documentation of Akola: location (Bhopalsagar tehsil, Chittorgarh), ~200 practitioners, allied communities, 14 traditional block designs, current tar/oil/rogan resist replacing mud (mud cracked), naphthol + red salt reds, ash dusting, indigo cold bath green->blue, boiling to remove tar, tools, challenges (fumes, water use, groundwater pollution). Intro inconsistently names Udaipur district. Fact-check 2026-10-14: page also explains naphthol/diazo salt coupling and records the zigzag phetiya border and kadhai-like boilers.

sources.title: Block printing the impermeable clay Dabu
sources.author: Craft Revival Trust
sources.publisher: Craft Revival Trust Archive via Google Arts & Culture
sources.notes: Documented at Deesa, Gujarat (not Akola). Paste of river-bed silt, local gum, lime, sugarcane molasses and water; kneaded by stamping over several days; strained; sawdust over wet paste; sun-dried until hard; dip-dyed; repeated per colour.

sources.title: Drying the dabu clay paste
sources.author: Craft Revival Trust
sources.publisher: Craft Revival Trust Archive via Google Arts & Culture
sources.notes: Documented at Bagru. Wet dabu dusted with beden (insect-eaten wheat-flour waste) to dry quickly and prevent smudging; dabu printing often done by women at home or in karkhanas.

sources.author: Geographical Indications Registry
sources.notes: Applicant Udhyam Protsahan Sansthan; filed 04-03-2022; Class 24 handicrafts; status Pre Examination (not registered) as of access date. Statement of Case listed but not read.

sources.title: Hand Block Printing of Akola, Rajasthan
sources.author: Global InCH (unattributed)
sources.publisher: Global InCH - International Journal of Living Heritage
sources.notes: Akola dabu types phetia and nangna; three resists of increasing strength: chuna/lime (kirana), mitti/mud, rait/sand; also describes a boiled bedja-gum + oil hot resist with ash dusting, metal blocks, naphthol/alizarin. Places Akola in Udaipur district. Fact-check: Phetia worn by Jat and Chaudhury women after childbirth or at weddings; nangna by Gujjar women (occasion not given).

sources.author: Global InCH (unattributed)

sources.title: Textile, object 88-16-37 (Bagru, mid-late 19th c.)
sources.author: Penn Museum
sources.publisher: University of Pennsylvania Museum of Archaeology and Anthropology
sources.notes: Cotton kagra (skirt) cloth from Bagru catalogued as block printed, mud resist, resist dyed, mordant dyed; resist areas pinkish possibly from red bleeding in washing.

sources.title: Indigo Dye Workshop
sources.author: Pratt's Textile Dye Garden
sources.notes: Clay resist works only with indigo because vat is cold and immersion brief; most natural dyes need heat and long immersion which would wash clay off; indigo turns green to blue as it oxygenates.

sources.title: Clay-Resist Indigo Dyeing
sources.author: Pratt's Textile Dye Garden
sources.notes: Generic (non-Indian) clay resist: let clay dry completely before submerging; fabric puckers as clay dries; re-dip possible while clay intact. Analogue evidence only.

sources.title: Fiber-Safe Extraction of Red Mordant Dyes from Hair Fibers
sources.author: Tiedemann, Erica J.; Yang, Yiqi
sources.publisher: Journal of the American Institute for Conservation 34(3):195-206
sources.notes: Alizarin forms six-membered chelate rings with aluminium; metal-dye lakes resist extraction by water and solvents. Supports shared alizarin-lake mechanism.

sources.title: Do or dye: New life for 500-year-old craft
sources.author: Ramdev, Darshana
sources.notes: Journalism on Alka Sharma (Aavaran founder) and a self-help group for Akola artisans set up in 2009; mud from riverbank mixed with lime and natural gum, babul seed resin binder, calcium hydroxide and pounded wheat chaff, mud soaked overnight; "five hundred year old craft"; origin tale presented as possibly untrue. Places Akola "near Udaipur".

sources.title: Kaisori discovers: The Dabu block prints of Akola
sources.author: Kaisori (unattributed)
sources.notes: Retailer field visit: arid region supplies mud, river water for washing, paste called "Hada", repeated resist and dye; largely mirrors S1.

sources.title: Mud In Textiles: The Art Of Block Printing in Rajasthan
sources.author: Jain, Anoushka
sources.notes: Secondary blog citing Kaur "DABU - A Unique Style of Mud Printing" (not accessible): kalidar, dolidar and gawarvali dabu recipes, kali mitti from dry pond soaked overnight, muslin straining, mardia pot, block woods, dye seeping through cracks.

sources.title: Dabu Printing
sources.author: Rao, Bindu Gopal
sources.publisher: bindugopalrao.com (first published in Apparel magazine, April 2019)
sources.notes: Journalist interview with an Akola printer: clay, chuna, wheat chaff, gum from acacia/babul; mud dug from a dry pond and soaked overnight; sawdust; hot-sun drying; repeat cycles; uneven cracks and veining; challenges. Fact-check: article spells the word "Dabana"; dated 3 May 2019 on the blog.

sources.title: Daboo Print: An Ancient Printing Technique from Rajasthan
sources.author: Utsavpedia (unattributed)
sources.notes: Akola as acknowledged origin; 675 AD claim; process incl. pre-printing with fast dyes; double/triple dabu; traditional dyes kashish, indigo, pomegranate.

sources.title: Craft Name: Dabu (Craft Katha)
sources.author: All India Artisans and Craftworkers Welfare Association (AIACA)
sources.notes: Black clay, lime and natural gum; "fermented mud paste"; light crackle effect; 5-15 days and 2-4 artisans per piece; attributes craft to Khatri community; claims GI tag in 2023 (contradicted by S5). Fact-check: page says "Khatris" and lists "Light crackle effect visible in resist areas" as an authenticity marker; no publication date (footer 2025).

sources.title: Dabu Block Printing
sources.author: Maiwa (unattributed)
sources.notes: Dabu described as "a cold-water resist" and a "mud-resist" using fine desert sand of Rajasthan, used during an indigo bath; reports certain patterns printed only on certain weaves of set width and length depending on the communities.

sources.title: The Story of Dabu Prints: Tradition, Craft, and Contemporary Style
sources.author: Team PeepulTree
sources.notes: Paste of chuna, gond and local clay; sawdust; sun-dry; dye; dry; wash; double/triple dabu; 8th-century claim.

sources.title: 'Bagru' - A Traditional Printing Technique of Rajasthan
sources.author: Raj, Sambaditya
sources.notes: Added by fact-check. Bagru-centred (not Akola). Scouring with a paste of cow dung, soda ash and sesame oil ("Hari sarana"); harda (myrobalan) wash whose tannic acid acts as mordant for the iron of the black (syahi); dabu = lime, "Bedhan" (worm-spoiled wheat flour) and black clay, mashed, left overnight, strained; Kaligar/Dolidar/Gawarbali dabu types; sawdust; indigo then pomegranate, then alum-water rinse to fix colour, alum quantity varying with dabu strength. Year from PDF metadata (2012); no peer review.

sources.title: Indian Block-Printed Textiles: Past and Present
sources.author: Rosenfield, Yael
sources.notes: Added by fact-check. Museum conservator essay (15 Nov 2016) with fieldwork at Bagru, Akola, Ajrakhpur, Sri Kalahasti: Dabu is "the most common resist used for indigo today", often showing crack lines where dye penetrated cracks in the resist; photo of an indigo vat at Akola (2015). Dung scouring and harde/alum/iron passages refer to Ajrakh/general practice, not Dabu.

concepts.title: Dabu mud-resist block printing
concepts.summary: Dabu is a mud-resist printing technique; blocks are dipped in a paste of mud, gum and lime and pressed onto fabric, and resist and dye are applied several times.
concepts.body_md:
Dabu is a mud-resist printing technique; blocks are dipped in a paste of mud, gum and lime and pressed onto fabric, and resist and dye are applied several times. [S1]

The name Dabu derives from dabaana, meaning to press. [S1, S2, S18]

Akola in Chittorgarh district is commonly acknowledged as the origin of the mud-resist Dabu style. [S19]

Dabu clay-resist printing is also documented by the Craft Revival Trust at Bagru (Rajasthan) and Deesa (Gujarat). [S3, S4]

Akola is described as a self-sufficient system for Dabu printing. [S1, S16]

concepts.summary: Akola is a village in Bhopalsagar tehsil, Chittorgarh district, about 52 km west of Chittorgarh.
concepts.body_md:
Akola is a village in Bhopalsagar tehsil, Chittorgarh district, about 52 km west of Chittorgarh. [S2, S10]

About 200 people practise the craft in Akola. [S1, S2]

Tradition holds that hundreds of years ago Rani Rathorji of Mewar established a village for the Chippa community on the banks of the Beduch river. [S1, S2]

Fabric is sourced from Kishangarh and pigments from Udaipur. [S1, S2]

Akola is also called Chhipo ka Akola. [S10]

concepts.title: Decline and revival
concepts.summary: Rajasthan once had many Dabu clusters; very few remain.
concepts.body_md:
Rajasthan once had many Dabu clusters; very few remain. [S1, S16]

Daboo almost died out in the era before independence because of cheap machine-printed alternatives; a designer quoted in 2019 says it has been revived by new-age designers. [S19, S18]

Aavaran set up a self-help group for Akola artisans in 2009, retaining the traditional process while introducing new motifs. [S15]

Aavaran and COS-V are cited as giving new direction to the craft. [S1]

concepts.summary: A fetiya was an 8-12 m cloth joined with one line of stitching, worn by Jat, Gadariya and Gujjar women, often with a bandhej lugda.
